1:
Every voice takes the opening phrase as a marker of the last things, and they differ only in how far they push it. Gill reports Kimchi referring it to the times of the Messiah, and applies it to the latter times of his spiritual reign yet to come. Clarke says some think the prophecy relates to the latter times of the world, when God shall finally deliver his people, and confesses that the figures employed are so lofty that their whole import cannot be restrained to any events before the Christian era; he adds that the whole is delivered in a very beautiful strain of poetry, and that what events are referred to is at present very uncertain. Ellicott takes the phrase to show the whole course of the world led up by providence to the great day, when the crooked shall be made straight and the rough places plain, so that the times of the restitution of all things will bring the people of God out of captivity and execute vengeance upon their enemies. Wesley takes both levels together: the days are when God shall bring the people out of the captivity by the hand of Cyrus, but the bringing back of the whole Israel of God by Christ is to be considered all along through the chapter, so that the first restoration is a type of the whole remnant that is saved.

Henry sets out the year in two halves. It shall be the year of the redeemed, since though the bondage of the people of God may be grievous and very long it shall not be everlasting; the bondage in Egypt ended in deliverance into the glorious liberty of the children of God, and that in Babylon shall likewise end well, while the Lord Jesus provides for the effectual redemption of enslaved souls from the dominion of sin, proclaiming the acceptable year, the jubilee, the release of debts and servants and the opening of the prison to those that were bound. There is a time fixed, Henry says, for bringing again the captivity of the children of God and redeeming them from the power of the grave, and it shall be the last day and the end of all time. And it shall be the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion, since though God may suffer the enemies of his people to prevail very far and for a long time, he will call them to account and lead captive those who led his people captive.

Calvin explains why the promise needed so much repeating. It was a thing difficult to be believed: when the body of the people was so mutilated, their name obliterated, their power abolished, the worship of God and the temple subverted, and no form of kingdom or even of civil government left, who could have thought that God had any concern for a people in such a wretched condition? So the prophet speaks at large of the restoration in order to confirm what would otherwise have been incredible.

Calvin also names the particular difficulty. The people were then hated by all nations and were the execration and the dregs of the whole world, so that as many nations as were under heaven were their enemies; a fall into despair was easy when they saw the whole world incensed against them, and they might argue that though God wished to redeem them there were so many obstacles that they must necessarily perish, since not only were the Assyrians enraged against them but they had found even greater hatred among their own neighbours. Calvin lists those neighbours one by one and observes that every access to their land was closed, so that it was hard to entertain any hope of deliverance though God encouraged them; and this is why the prophet declares that God would be the judge of the whole world.
2:
Who the gathered nations are is answered by the scheme each commentator holds. Gill sets aside the identification with the confederacy defeated in the reign of Jehoshaphat, and offers instead either the power he identifies with the Gog and Magog of Ezekiel, gathered with many other nations against the converted people, or else all the antichristian kings gathered to the battle of the great day. Wesley keeps his double reading: in the type, all those nations that have oppressed the people, and in the antitype all nations that have been enemies to Christ and the church. Keil and Delitzsch say the prophet speaks not of events belonging to his own time but of the dispersion of the whole covenant nation among the heathen, only completely effected at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans and continuing to this day; and they refuse the inference one scholar drew from it, since the prophet could assume the dispersion as a truth well known, having been foretold by Moses even though he had not expressed it in his earlier threatenings.

The valley divides them more sharply. Clarke says flatly that there is no such valley in the land, so that the word must be symbolical, signifying the judgment of God; he reports a suggestion that it may mean some place where a conqueror should gain a great battle discomfiting the ancient enemies of the people. Ellicott gives the history: some fifty years before the prophet, the kingdom had been menaced by an imposing confederacy of hostile tribes, a national fast was proclaimed, and the king routed the enemy in a valley in the wilderness of Tekoa; the victory was an occasion of immense exultation and seems to supply the imagery for the day of the Lord. He notes that the name was at some period given to another valley, but is here used rather in its grammatical meaning, as the scene of the divine judgment, the words signifying the valley where the Lord judges. Calvin reports the same view, that many think the place intended is the valley where the king fought a large army with few people and wonderfully succeeded, so that the people presented thanks to God there and gave a name to the spot.

Calvin sets the promise in a larger frame. He compares the word of Haggai that the glory of the second temple should be greater than that of the first, and observes that such promises were not confined to four or five ages but meant that the favour of God would continue to the coming of Christ; so here God will become the complete Redeemer of his people, and when the whole world rises against him he will yet prevail, so that whoever attempts to hinder the restoration of the church shall by no means succeed.

The casting of lots is the sharpest indignity. Gill takes it that they cast lots not only for the land but for the persons, playing at dice for how many captives each soldier should have, and cites the number Josephus gives for those carried away. Wesley says it was customary with conquerors to divide captives by lot. Ellicott says the oppressors treated them as chattels and purchased a night of revelry with the captives they had taken. Clarke reads the next clause literally and darkly, the children sold by their oppressors, used for the basest purposes and bartered for the necessaries or luxuries of life. Calvin distinguishes a twofold injury: some take the prophet to say that boys were prostituted, but he prefers that the enemies sold them at a mean price to gratify their gluttony or lust, so that the reproach lies in their being set to sale as the offscourings of mankind, while the second injury is that the price obtained was afterwards spent on gluttony and whoredom, though the people so treated were sacred to God.
4:
The question is heard as God identifying himself with the injured. Gill takes the two cities and the coast as near neighbours and implacable enemies, and reads the question two ways: what have you to do with me, to be called by my name, and what have you to do with my people, to distress them. Ellicott renders it more sharply, what are ye to me, and says God identifies himself with his people and threatens retaliation for the wrongs inflicted on them; he notes that these had oppressed the people in the time of the judges and would do so again, and that the coastal people were to the last their inveterate enemies; but could they in the end measure strength with God? Clarke puts it in a phrase, that they who touch the people touch God, and reads the next clause as incredulity, whether they think to avenge themselves upon the Almighty.

Calvin makes the unprovokedness the aggravation. Had they been provoked, some excuse might have been made, but since they made war of their own accord the wrong was doubled; and God here does not merely undertake the protection of his people but defends his own cause, asking whether he owes them anything or lies under any obligation to them. The question, on his reading, is whether they can boast of any just pretence for making war on his people, and the answer is that no wrong had been done them which they could now retaliate, so that they attacked through their own wickedness, impelled only by avarice or cruelty. Wesley puts it as a series of questions, whether God has done them any wrong which they avenge on his people, and whether they think they have to do with a poor oppressed people about whom he is unconcerned.

The silver and gold are claimed in two ways. Gill takes them either as belonging to God absolutely or as what he had bestowed on his people. Ellicott is more precise: they are called his as being the property of his people, not as dedicated to the service of the Temple, and he cites an earlier reign in which invaders carried away all the substance found in the house of the king. Clarke and Wesley take the opposite view, Clarke naming the spoiling of the temple and the carrying of its vessels into the temple of a foreign god, Wesley taking the silver as vessels dedicated to the divine service. Calvin canvasses both and prefers the temple: many extend the plunder generally to the whole wealth of the people, but he thinks the complaint special, and renders the word temples rather than palaces, so that these neighbours profaned the vessels by dedicating them to their idols, adorning their idols with spoils taken from the only true God. He explains how they came by them: they were at first ill disposed, then gaped after booty and showed themselves openly enemies when they saw hope of gain, helping the invaders with provisions so as to partake of the spoil, which the conquerors were glad to grant since the carriage of the metal would have been tedious.

The selling to a distant people is the last charge. Clarke and Ellicott both identify the buyers with the descendants of Javan, whose traffic in slaves Ellicott calls enormous and whom the trading city is elsewhere said to have supplied with the persons of men. Clarke reads the purpose as sending them as far off as possible, so that it should be impossible for them to return and reclaim the land they had been dispossessed of. Calvin says the same, and finds in it the clearest evidence of cruelty, since the sellers took care to drive the wretched men far away and leave no road home. Gill corrects one detail, that the children are not children in age, as Kimchi supposed, but the inhabitants.
7:
The raising up is read as a return. Gill takes it of bringing them back to their own land from the places where they had dwelt in obscurity, as if buried in graves, so that the restoration will be as life from the dead. Clarke and Wesley both name a historical fulfilment: it is said that Alexander and his successors set at liberty many who had been sold into Greece, and Clarke adds that many likely returned from various lands on the publication of the edict of Cyrus.

Calvin presses the question the others pass over. When has this prediction been fulfilled? The people never returned to their own country in the sense the words seem to require: shortly after the return from exile they were diminished in various ways, and grievous calamities followed which consumed the greatest part of them, the land never ceasing to be distressed by continual wars until Jerusalem was destroyed and the people almost wholly consumed. He reports the allegorical answer, that the prophet speaks of apostles and martyrs driven by persecution into different parts, and calls it a strained view; his own answer is that the gathering meant is spiritual.

The reversal in the next verse is what Calvin dwells on. The neighbours had sold the people; now who is to be the seller? God himself will take the office, so that the servitude is legitimate and the buyers differ from the robbers who had unjustly seized what was not their own; the manner of the sale is so described as to say that God is the author of the change and the thing done by his authority, as if he had interposed his own name. On the distant buyers Calvin takes the name as a part put for the whole, designating the eastern nations, and observes that these lay very far from the sea of the sellers, being known as nearly neighbours to the Indians, so that the sellers are driven to the most distant countries.

The historical fulfilment is canvassed in detail. Gill says it is thought to have been literally fulfilled when thirty thousand of the chief city were sold for slaves on its capture, some being put into the hands of the people who were then in friendship with the conqueror. Clarke gives the same number from Arrian, adds that another king destroyed Sidon and subdued the other cities of that coast, and reports Calmet for the further detail that in all these wars the people who obeyed the Persians did not neglect to purchase slaves from that coast, whom they sold again to the Sabeans. Ellicott takes a different line, referring the selling to two earlier kings under whom the coastal people came, who may have sold them to the Sabeans on the Persian Gulf, by whom they would have been passed on to India, and adding that they were also sold in great numbers by the Grecian conquerors in the time of the Maccabees. Calvin, quoting a note to the same effect, dates the fulfilment to the same age, when the affairs of the people were in a flourishing state and the powers of that coast had been reduced by successive conquerors.
9:
The proclamation is heard by most as irony. Gill leaves it open whether the heralds are sent seriously or ironically, but says what follows seems spoken in the latter way to the enemies of the church, though it may be interpreted as spoken seriously to the people of God. Henry takes it as a challenge given to the enemies of the kingdom to do their worst: to signify that God is preparing war against them they are called on to prepare war against him, all the forces of the nations summoned to join in confederacy against God and his people, like the older summons to associate and gird themselves and yet be broken to pieces. Clarke reads it the same way and carries the summons further: let them call all the tillers of the ground to their assistance instead of labouring in the field, let every peasant become a soldier and every agricultural implement an offensive weapon, so that the weak, being well armed, may confidently say they are strong; and yet, when thus collected and armed, God will bring down their mighty ones, which is how Clarke would render the following verse.

Ellicott renders the opening command literally and finds a solemnity in it. The words mean to sanctify war, which was to be taken up deliberately and after due religious rites, according to the customs of the nations; the enemies are thus challenged, or rather summoned, to a trial of strength with God at what he calls a typical Armageddon.

Calvin sets aside one reading and defends another. Some think the words were announced lest the people, terrified by their evils, should become wholly dejected, so that God placed this dreadful spectacle before their eyes that they might prepare and strengthen themselves to endure, abiding firm in the hope that he would be the defender of his church. Calvin does not doubt that the prophet instead continues the same discourse and denounces war on the heathen nations which had troubled the church; and he explains why so lively a representation was necessary. The ungodly are moved by no threats and laugh to scorn all the judgments of God, while the faithful, yielding to their evils, can hardly raise their minds even when God promises to help them; so unless the matter were set forth as painted before their eyes they would not have experienced the power of consolation. Seeing as it were with their eyes what the prophet sets forth by a figure, they were more effectually impressed and felt more assured that God would at length become their deliverer.

Whom the proclamation reaches is answered by each commentator scheme. Gill takes the decree to be proclaimed among the nations, to their terror and the comfort of the people, and returns the reader to the armies gathered for destruction in the valley named earlier. Wesley names three successive empires. Henry allows the notice of judgment to refer to particular conquerors and to the antichrist and all the proud enemies of the Christian church, but reports that some of the best interpreters, ancient and modern, take the scope of these verses to be the day of the last judgment, set forth under the similitude of God making war on the enemies of his kingdom and gathering in the harvest of the earth, both similitudes being found in the Revelation. Henry also recalls the older word that the Lord reigns and comes to judge the earth, and says the prophet will have it published to all nations in the same way.
10:
The opening command reverses a familiar promise, and the commentators all notice it. Calvin observes that Isaiah and Micah, prophesying of the kingdom of Christ, said that swords should be beaten into pruninghooks and spears into plowshares, and that Joel here inverts the sentence. Those words were figurative, showing that the world would be at peace when Christ reconciled men to God and taught them to cultivate brotherly kindness; Joel says instead that there would be turbulent commotions everywhere, so that no use would be made of the plough or the pruninghook, husbandmen ceasing from their labour and the land remaining waste, as when a whole country is exposed to violence. Ellicott looks the other way down the same road, recalling that Micah foresaw the reversal of this order once the victory of the Lord was achieved, and the weapons of offence resumed their peaceful character. Gill reads the command as a general levy: not only soldiers trained in military discipline are to appear, but husbandmen and vinedressers must leave their fields and turn the instruments of husbandry into weapons, pleading no want of armour. Calvin presses the matter of exemption. Excuses on the ground of age or disease formerly availed when soldiers were collected, and a sick man was dismissed; here God will excuse none, but will draw even the sick from their beds. Wesley reads the weak man’s boast as a charge to put on strength and valour, and lets none be absent from this war.

Gill takes the next call as an order to muster from divers parts into one place, noting that where the Targum and Kimchi give gather yourselves together, Jarchi, following Menachem, changes a letter and reads make ye haste. The mighty ones divide the readers. Ellicott makes them the enemy’s own champions, called thy because Jehovah had summoned them to take arms against him in the final conflict. Wesley makes them God’s instruments instead, the mighty warriors he would use successively to punish the oppressors of his church, brought down toward Jerusalem. Calvin observes that though the prophet uses the singular number he refers to the whole earth: whatever enemies there may be to his people, however strong, God will cut them down.

On the waking of the nations Clarke is briefest and most sweeping: the valley is any place where God may choose to display his judgments against his enemies. Gill keeps it geographical, observing that the land of Judea was higher than other countries, so that men are said to go up to it though one usually goes down a valley; the enemies, roused from their security, invade the holy land and descend into the place appointed for their ruin. Wesley names the invaders outright, the Assyrians first under Salmaneser and next under Sennacherib, both of whom came up to the valley. Calvin declines the detail and holds to the pattern: God does not immediately succour his servants but rests as though he did not regard their troubles, so as to try their patience, deferring punishment until the wickedness of his enemies has been completed, and then ascending his tribunal.

Two metaphors close the passage, and Clarke and Calvin agree in naming them, the reaping of a harvest and the gathering and treading of grapes. Calvin adds the reason for the long delay from Abraham’s day, when the wickedness of the Canaanites was not yet completed and four hundred years were named; here it has multiplied and is overflowing. Ellicott hears the prophet crowd his metaphors together, judgment seat and harvest and vintage, and reads the harvest-time as the end of the world, with angel-reapers told to put in the sickle. Gill makes the reapers the mighty ones already sent to execute the vengeance. Wesley runs the sickle through history instead, from Tiglath Pilneser to Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, Alexander and the Romans, and only then to the final judgment.
14:
The doubled cry draws out the expositors’ care over the name of the place. Gill holds the valley of decision to be the same as the valley of Jehoshaphat already named, which shows that no valley actually bearing the name is intended, but a place so called from the judgments of God done in it. It is the valley of decision, he says with Kimchi and Jarchi, because there the judgment will be determined and the controversy between God and his people’s enemies ended; the Vulgate Latin version gives the valley of concision, since the gathered nations will be cut to pieces there; others the valley of threshing, alluding to the time of Jehoshaphat, when the Moabites and Ammonites were threshed in the valley of Berachah. Clarke agrees, renders the doubled word as crowds upon crowds, and allows either decision or excision. Ellicott hears the exclamation as the prophet’s own astonishment, the command having gone forth and been obeyed; Gill likewise makes it the prophet breaking out into a pathetic exclamation at the sight.

Calvin asks why the words are multiplied, and answers from the hearers’ state. The devastation of the church might have taken away all hope from God’s servants: who could have said it could be restored when it was so miserably wasted? The people were so scattered that the name of Israel was of no account, the constitution of the church dissolved, and all might have said they were given up to a thousand modes of destruction. The repetition is therefore not superfluous: the prophet testifies in various forms of words that God would abide faithful and had power enough to vivify a dead people. Calvin adds that the prophet assumes the character of a herald, and grants how ridiculous the summons must have looked, his doctrine being laughed to scorn even at Jerusalem; the power of the prediction was hidden, and showed itself only at last.

On the darkening of the lights the readings part. Gill and Clarke both take the figure politically, Clarke most fully: high and mighty states are eclipsed and ruined, while the stars, the petty states, princes and governors, withdraw their shining, withholding their influence and tribute from the kingdoms to which they belonged and setting up as independent governors. Calvin does not expound it again, having explained it earlier, but recalls its purpose: the figurative expressions describe the terrible judgment of God to shake off the indifference of men, who despise all threatening unless the Lord storms their hearts.

The roaring from Zion is where Calvin locates the turn of the passage. All that went before served only to spread terror, but the prophet’s purpose was to console the faithful and relieve their troubles. Roaring is ascribed to God because he elsewhere compares himself to a lion who suffers not the prey to be taken from him but defends it with all his fierceness. God had for a time been still while the nations plundered his people at their pleasure; now he will not always conceal himself. Though heaven and earth raise opposition he will prevail; if the elements shake, what will men do? Wesley makes the same comparison briefly: the roar astonishes the enemy as the lion astonishes the weaker beasts of the forest. Gill has Christ the Lamb appear as the Lion of the tribe of Judah, uttering his voice in judgment on behalf of Zion. Clarke adds that the temple and worship are reestablished there first, and that amid great commotions in powerful empires God’s people are unmoved. Ellicott alone reaches outside the book, noting that Amos opens his appeal with these words, that the majestic roar expresses the irresistible utterance of the Lord’s judgment, and that Paul wrote of the Lord descending from heaven with a shout; he takes the temporal success of the Jews to be blended here with the final triumph in the judgment day.
17:
Calvin reads the promise that they shall know as a promise of a particular kind of knowing. God’s favour had been so hidden during the people’s afflictions that they could not but think themselves forsaken. His word ought to suffice in the greatest evils, yet unless he really appears we are confounded and ask where his power is. So he distinguishes a twofold knowledge, that of faith received from the word and that of experience derived from actual enjoyment. The faithful ever acknowledge that salvation is laid up for them in God, yet sometimes they stagger and are tossed here and there, not knowing him as their Father by enjoyment. It is this real knowledge the prophet promises; and Calvin turns it back on the reader, for he spoke that the godly might cast all their cares on God before the accomplishment came, entertaining good hope of his favour though he should not manifestly help.

The others describe that knowing from its evidences. Gill makes the holy mountain the church, God’s dwelling place, and says his presence will be discerned by the destruction of their enemies and his protection of them, so that they know his inhabitation experimentally. Clarke says it is by those judgments and the support given to themselves that they know the all-conquering Jehovah has again taken up residence in Jerusalem. Wesley dates the then to the destruction of the enemies, the saving of the remnant and the coming of the Messiah.

The clause about strangers divides them along the chapter’s usual line. Clarke takes it of a restoration of the Jews to their own land, with holiness to the Lord for their motto and no impure people permitted to enter or pass through the city; he refers it to Gospel times and calls it a promise not yet fulfilled. Wesley makes Jerusalem the church of Christ and the strangers the unclean. Ellicott turns it inward: the strangers are the aliens who had hitherto oppressed, like the spots and wrinkles that would defile the bride, the Church of God. Henry gives the plainest account of their reach: they are accomplished in part in the kingdom of grace and in the graces of its faithful subjects, but fully only in the kingdom of glory; as to the Jewish church he knows of no event answering their extent, and whatever peace it enjoyed was but a figure of better things reserved for later readers. Gill reports an interpreter who applied such prophecies to the times of the Maccabees, owning them an emblem of better times under the Gospel. Calvin enters a caution: when the prophets so splendidly extol God’s blessings they do not mean to fill the godly with thoughts about eating and drinking, though profane men lay hold on such passages as though the Lord meant to gratify their appetite; God’s children differ much from swine, and he does not fill the faithful with earthly things.

Clarke and Ellicott both work at the valley. Clarke reads the wine and milk as a poetic expression for great fertility, and refers the fountain to the typical waters traced by Ezekiel, pointing to the grace of the Gospel flowing from Jerusalem. He then argues that Shittim, in the plains of Moab beyond Jordan, cannot be literal, since no stream could flow from the temple across Jordan to that plain; the valley must be symbolical, like the valley of Jehoshaphat. Ellicott renders the name as acacias and makes the place symbolical of the dry world where trees lack moisture, and of the heathen who shall yet be covered with the knowledge of the Lord. Wesley keeps Shittim a place in the plains of Moab and lets the spiritual waters flow down to the barren Gentiles; in the fountain he hears an allusion to waters conveyed from a spring through conduit pipes toward the altar, a shadow of the purifying blood of Christ.
19:
The two names that close the prophecy are read by most as representative, not merely national. Gill says these two nations, implacable enemies of Israel, stand for the future adversaries of the church of Christ. Wesley says the same, Egypt standing for all who carry it toward the church as Egypt did toward Israel, and Edom for all of that character, an implacable enemy to Judah in his distress. Ellicott stays with the sentiment of the first hearers: Egypt and Edom always excited abhorrence in Jewish hearts, the memory of the exile being fresh and keen; the detestation of the false and cruel-hearted kinsmen is recalled by Obadiah and in the psalm asking the Lord to remember the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, how they said, Down with it, even to the ground.

Where the innocent blood was shed is a real division. Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase of the offenders’ own territory, the land of the Egyptians and Edomites and not of the Judaeans, dating them: in Egypt of old by the command to slay the Hebrew boys, and in Edom when it threw off the dominion of Judah; both lands had thereby become types of the world power in its hostility to God. Calvin knows this reading and what supports it, since many fled to Egypt and Idumea for refuge in times of distress, so that the charge would be of slaying fugitives rather than sheltering them; but he prefers to place the slaughters in Judea itself, since God had consecrated that land and to pollute it with unjust slaughters was the more atrocious crime. Clarke keeps only the contrast: while peace and plenty crown God’s people all their enemies shall be as a wilderness; Calvin draws it harder, since though Judea would abound in honey and milk and wine, these would remain barren.

On the permanence promised to Judah, Calvin says why it is added. It would be but a small thing for the church to be redeemed unless God kept it safe under his own power; the ungodly sometimes flourish for a time though already doomed, but the fruit of this redemption is eternal, God following his church with perpetual favour. Keil and Delitzsch make the dwelling a poetical expression for being inhabited, land and city alike personified. Gill and Clarke both read a double reference, to converted Jews dwelling in their own land and never more carried captive, and to the church continuing while persecuting churches are annihilated.

The closing promise divides on whether the cleansing falls on the enemies or on the people. Clarke renders it as vengeance, God avenging the slaughter and martyrdom of his people, so that persecuting nations and churches come at last under vindictive justice. Ellicott reports the same rendering from the Greek version but holds the promise rather to indicate the extension of God’s pardon to those hitherto unpardoned. Gill takes it that way too, against the reading he finds in the Targum, Judah and Jerusalem being the immediate antecedents whose iniquities the Lord will forgive. Wesley has the purging done by the spirit of sanctification and by free pardon. Calvin canvasses two constructions: that God forgives all other wrongs but not the shedding of his people’s blood, which he thinks too forced, and, as the simpler, that God will now cleanse the pollutions he had not hitherto cleansed, which had become as it were putrid, that his people may shine pure. Keil and Delitzsch decline both halves of the question: the verse announces no further punishment but simply closes the proclamation. Clarke ends where the prophet does, noting that this book closes almost as Ezekiel closes, the one naming the city The Lord Is There, the other saying the Lord dwelleth in Zion; Ellicott hears in it the Lord reigning over a raging world unconscious of him, his redeemed secure under his eternal rule.
